references.text: This verse in Leviticus also prescribes the death penalty for a man who commits adultery with another man's wife, which directly aligns with the law in Deuteronomy 22:22.
This verse forbids sexual relations with another man's wife and calls it impurity, underscoring the seriousness of the prohibition against adultery.
Ezekiel describes the punishment for women who break marriage vows, including judgment for adultery, illustrating the application of this law.
The expression "you shall purge the evil from Israel" is used here and in several places in Deuteronomy as a standard formula for removing sin from the people.
The same expression "you shall purge the evil from your midst" is used here in connection with the death penalty, showing a consistent legal principle.
The scribes and Pharisees refer to the Mosaic Law when they bring a woman caught in adultery to Jesus, noting that the law commanded stoning.
Proverbs warns that whoever commits adultery destroys themselves and will reap shame and disgrace.
The story of Judah and Tamar shows that the death penalty by burning was demanded for a woman accused of harlotry, reflecting early practice of severe punishment for such offenses.
